question: A 25-year-old man consults for jaundice. He practices bodybuilding and has injected anabolic steroids substitutes for 17alkalkyl, three weeks before. For a tonsillitis he had taken amoxicillin-clavulanic acid which he removed 15 days ago. Analytical: AST 1200 IU / L (normal upper limit, lsn 40), ALT 1300 IU / L (lsn 40), GGT 150 IU / L (lsn 50), alkaline phosphatase 180 IU / L (lsn 105), total bililrubin 4 , 8 mg / dL with direct bilirubin predominance. Serology of virus B: Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc positive. Ultrasound suggests grade I steatosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Anabolic steroids use" -> "liver stress" -> "elevated AST and ALT" -> "direct bilirubin predominance" -> "anabolic steroid hepatitis" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid use" -> "possible liver injury" -> "elevated liver enzymes" -> "direct bilirubin predominance" -> "hepatitis by amoxicillin-clavulanic acid" -> 60%
CHAIN: "Positive Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc" -> "past hepatitis B infection" -> "unlikely acute hepatitis B" -> "other causes more likely" -> 30%
CHAIN: "Bodybuilding" -> "anabolic steroid use" -> "liver enzyme elevation" -> "direct bilirubin predominance" -> "anabolic steroid hepatitis" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Ultrasound grade I steatosis" -> "mild fatty liver" -> "unlikely cause of severe enzyme elevation" -> "other causes more likely" -> 40%
CHAIN: "Drug use history" -> "possible drug-induced cholestasis" -> "elevated bilirubin" -> "elevated liver enzymes" -> "cholestasis due to drugs" -> 50%
analysis: The patient presents with jaundice and significantly elevated liver enzymes (AST and ALT), which are indicative of hepatocellular injury. The history of anabolic steroid use is a strong risk factor for drug-induced liver injury, particularly hepatocellular injury, which aligns with the elevated transaminases. The serology for hepatitis B shows immunity (Anti-HBs positive) and past infection (Anti-HBc positive), ruling out acute hepatitis B. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid can cause liver injury, but it is more commonly associated with cholestatic or mixed patterns rather than the predominantly hepatocellular pattern seen here. The ultrasound finding of grade I steatosis is mild and not typically associated with such high transaminase levels. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is anabolic steroid-induced hepatitis.
